laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe and include the death penalty, life imprisonment and heavy fines. Don't use or carry any illegal drugs, including illegal prescription medication. Carrying certain prescription drugs can result in heavy fines and long jail sentences (see 'Health').
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: If you're involved in a legal dispute, you won't be allowed to leave Taiwan until the dispute is settled. This includes minor offences. You may be detained on arrival if you have an outstanding arrest warrant in Taiwan. Legal processes can be long. Local authorities won't accept bonds or deposits to guarantee court appearances.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Some prescription medications are illegal in Taiwan. Authorities may jail or fine you for carrying these medications. If you plan to take medication, check if it's legal in Taiwan. Taiwan Customs gives advice on limits and documents you'll need.
laws.heading: Medications

laws.rule: If you plan to drive in Taiwan, you must get an International Driving Permit (IDP) before you arrive. You can drive for up to 30 days with an IDP and a current Australian licence (digital driver's licences may not be accepted). If you plan to stay longer, apply for an extension at the nearest motor vehicle office in Taiwan. Check Taiwan’s Highway Bureau for information on how to apply for a Taiwanese Driver's Licence.
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: A foreign visitor with a foreign drone registration, inspection certificate and remote pilot licence must have them validated by the CAA before flying in the Taipei Flight Information Region. Validation lasts up to six months. Flights stay at or below 400 ft, not between sunset and sunrise, and not over crowds.
laws.heading: Foreign drone validation and limits
laws.penalty_signal: Breaches of the registration rules can bring a flying ban and a fine of NT$30,000 to NT$150,000, and in serious cases seizure of the drone (no AUD rate on file).

laws.rule: The duty-free allowance is 1.5 litres of alcoholic drink per person, any number of bottles (up from 1 litre from 25 January 2025). The Customs Administration notice says passengers aged 18 or over; a Taipei Customs page says aged 20 or over, so the age is unsettled between the two pages.
laws.penalty_signal: Undeclared liquor over the allowance is confiscated and fined under the Tobacco and Alcohol Administration Act.

laws.rule: The duty-free tobacco allowance (Taipei Customs, aged 20 or over) is 200 cigarettes, or 25 cigars, or 1 pound of tobacco, or 200 designated tobacco products that passed the Ministry of Health and Welfare's health risk assessment. The page does not mention e-cigarettes or unapproved heated tobacco, so ask Customs before bringing them.

Each person may carry at most NT$100,000 (about A$4,360 at TWD 22.95 per A$1, RBA 30 Oct 2026) or RMB 20,000 (about A$4,270 at CNY 4.6877 per A$1) into or out of Taiwan. Any amount above those limits is not allowed even if declared. Other foreign currency, and negotiable securities, over USD 10,000 (about A$14,200 at USD 0.7040 per A$1) must be declared; once declared there is no limit.
laws.penalty_signal: Cash over the limits that is not declared is subject to confiscation.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: Foreign visitors holding a foreign drone registration, inspection certificate and remote pilot licence must have them validated by the CAA before flying in the Taipei FIR; validation lasts up to six months. Foreign legal entities that need to film must apply through a Taiwanese agency or entity.

items.text: Not yet checked: no public CAA directory of drone operators was found on the pages read.

Drones over 250 g owned by individuals are registered and carry their registration number (fee NT$50 per drone; no AUD rate on file). Flights stay at or below 400 ft, not between sunset and sunrise, and not over crowds.

Foreign nationals with a valid drone registration, inspection certificate and remote pilot licence from their own government submit an application form, passport copy and proof, and are certified before flying; non-English documents need a Chinese translation. The validation lasts up to six months. A CAA FAQ says foreign legal entities that need to film must apply through a domestic government agency, school or legal entity.

layers.authority: National Park Service, Ministry of the Interior (Yushan, Taroko and Shei-Pa National Park headquarters), through the Hike Smart Taiwan service
layers.process: Some mountain routes in Yushan, Taroko and Shei-Pa national parks are ecological protection areas that need a park entry permit, applied for online at Hike Smart Taiwan. The three parks share the system but each reviews its own applications and each park needs its own application. Applications are open 07:00 to 23:00 Taiwan time. Yushan pauses applications during its lottery hour (15:00 to 16:00). Permits and their registration are free of charge. The parks lie across several counties (Taroko's FAQ names Hualien County's Xiulin police); the county tree is not built yet, so this is held at country level.

layers.authority: National Police Agency (mountain entry permit) with the park headquarters
layers.process: A separate mountain entry permit (also called a police mountain permit) covers restricted mountain areas and is managed by the National Police Agency. Some routes need both permits, some only one, some none. Taroko lists, for example, Mt Nanhu and Mt Qilai as needing both, Zhuilu Old Road as park permit only, and Hehuan Main Peak and Shakadang Trail as needing none. After a park permit is approved, the applicant can send the details on to the police system online; Taroko's FAQ says this is available 5 to 30 days (in one line 'working days') before the hike, the online police form is in Chinese only, and a permit can also be bought in person at a police station near the trailhead. Yushan says an approved group can download its park permit 5 days before entry.

Yushan's Paiyun Lodge (the hut on the main Yushan route) is allocated by lottery about one month before the entry date. A separate advance quota for foreigners can be applied for from 4 months to 35 days before the climb date: 24 places a day, Sunday to Thursday, not on national holidays, and at most 2 local people per team as guides or interpreters. Lodging is NT$480 a person a night (about A$20.92, RBA rate of 30 October 2026, TWD 22.95 per A$1). Under-18s need a parent's or guardian's consent form.

Shei-Pa reserves 24 places a day for foreigners at each of Qika Hut, Saliujiu Hut and Jiujiu Hut, Sunday to Thursday outside continuous national holidays. The foreign window is 4 months to 65 days before the entry date, for foreign tourists with a foreign address (students and foreigners living in Taiwan use the standard application). A team has up to 12 members and may include locals (1 local for 1 to 5 foreigners, 2 for 6 to 10, at most 4 locals in the foreign quota per hut). Unfilled places pass to the standard application. The guideline PDF is undated.

Taroko charges NT$200 (about A$8.71 at TWD 22.95 per A$1, RBA 30 October 2026) to enter Zhuilu Old Road, cash on arrival at the trailhead. Taroko's FAQ (dated 2019) gives windows of 7 to 30 days before entry for most mountain routes, 3 to 30 days for single-day Mt Yangtou and Mt Bilu, and 1 to 30 days for Zhuilu Old Road (up to 3 pm the working day before). Some routes have daily quotas.
